title: Sepsis: Infection Plus New Organ Dysfunction
bottomLine: Sepsis is a time-critical syndrome of infection with acute organ dysfunction. Recognize a change from baseline—altered mentation, hypotension, rising oxygen need, oliguria, poor perfusion, lactate elevation, or other organ failure—activate the sepsis pathway, obtain appropriate cultures without delaying treatment, give antimicrobials and resuscitation as ordered, and repeatedly reassess perfusion and response.
recognize: Possible infection plus new organ dysfunction is more important than fever alone
Older, immunocompromised, or severely ill patients may be afebrile or hypothermic
Tachypnea, confusion, low urine output, mottling, hypotension, or increasing oxygen need can be early bedside clues
assess: Airway, breathing, SpO2, BP/MAP, pulse, mental status, skin perfusion, urine output, temperature
Identify suspected source and recent antibiotics, procedures, devices, immune suppression, or hospitalization
Trend lactate and other organ markers when ordered; reassess after fluids/vasopressors/antimicrobials
actions: Activate the facility sepsis pathway promptly
Obtain ordered blood/source cultures before antibiotics when feasible without causing harmful delay
Administer appropriate antimicrobials and fluids according to the treatment plan
Escalate persistent hypotension or hypoperfusion for vasopressor and critical-care support
diagnostics: Cultures help target therapy but negative cultures do not exclude sepsis
Lactate is a perfusion/risk marker, not a stand-alone sepsis diagnosis
Source imaging is selected according to the clinical problem and should not delay stabilization
medicationSafety: Antimicrobial therapy should be reassessed and narrowed/de-escalated when microbiology and clinical data allow
Large-volume fluids can harm patients with overload risk, so response-guided reassessment matters
Vasoactive infusions require close hemodynamic monitoring and setting-specific competency
teaching: Teach patients recovering from infection or sepsis to seek urgent care for worsening confusion, breathing difficulty, severe weakness, low urine output, or rapidly worsening illness
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes deterioration, activates the sepsis pathway, collects ordered specimens, administers authorized antibiotics/fluids, and reassesses. Vasopressor titration and advanced resuscitation depend on setting and scope.
examTrap: Waiting for high fever or a positive blood culture before treating a hypotensive confused patient with suspected infection as possible sepsis.
oneLinePearl: Sepsis is infection plus failing organs—recognize the change and act early.
sourceBasis: CDC Hospital Sepsis Program Core Elements

title: Anaphylaxis: Epinephrine First, Airway and Circulation in Parallel
bottomLine: Anaphylaxis is a rapidly evolving systemic allergic emergency. Give intramuscular epinephrine promptly when criteria are met, activate emergency support, manage airway/oxygenation and circulation, repeat epinephrine as directed for persistent symptoms, and monitor for recurrence. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are not substitutes for epinephrine.
recognize: Airway swelling, stridor, wheeze, respiratory distress
Hypotension, syncope, shock
Widespread hives/flushing/angioedema may occur but skin findings can be absent
Severe GI symptoms can accompany systemic reactions
assess: Airway/voice/tongue swelling, breathing, SpO2, BP/perfusion, mental status
Identify likely trigger and time of exposure without delaying treatment
Monitor continuously for response and recurrent symptoms
actions: Give IM epinephrine in the recommended anterolateral thigh location per emergency protocol
Call emergency/rapid response and position according to hemodynamics and breathing
Provide oxygen, IV access, fluids, bronchodilator, or additional therapies as ordered
Prepare for advanced airway management if swelling or respiratory failure progresses
diagnostics: Anaphylaxis is primarily a clinical diagnosis; do not delay epinephrine for laboratory confirmation
Serum tryptase may support later evaluation in selected cases but is not needed to start treatment
medicationSafety: Epinephrine is first-line; antihistamines treat selected skin symptoms but do not reverse shock or airway edema
Observe for recurrent symptoms according to severity and treatment response
teaching: Carry prescribed epinephrine, know how and when to use it, replace expired devices, and obtain allergy follow-up and an emergency action plan
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN emergency medication authority depends on setting and standing orders, but suspected anaphylaxis requires immediate activation of the emergency pathway. Do not delay epinephrine while waiting for an antihistamine order when an authorized anaphylaxis protocol applies.
examTrap: Giving diphenhydramine first to a hypotensive wheezing patient with generalized allergic symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Anaphylaxis: epinephrine first; antihistamines are supporting actors.

title: S. aureus and MRSA: A Positive Blood Culture Is Never a Throwaway Finding
bottomLine: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia can seed valves, bone, joints, devices and other organs. Treat it as clinically significant, administer directed IV therapy exactly as ordered, obtain follow-up cultures and source-control evaluation, and report persistent fever, new murmur, focal pain, neurologic change, or device infection.
recognize: S. aureus in blood culture commonly represents true bacteremia rather than simple contamination
Potential sources include skin/soft tissue, vascular catheters, wounds, bone/joint infection, and endocarditis
MRSA status affects antimicrobial selection and infection-control precautions
assess: Vitals, perfusion, skin/wounds, IV/central-line sites, new focal bone/joint pain, cardiac/neuro symptoms
Trend repeat cultures, renal function, CBC, and drug-specific levels/labs as ordered
Assess for source-control needs
actions: Administer active antimicrobial therapy on schedule
Use indicated contact precautions according to facility policy
Remove or manage infected devices/source when ordered
Escalate persistent bacteremia or metastatic infection signs
diagnostics: Repeat blood cultures document clearance
Echocardiography evaluates endocarditis risk
Imaging targets focal symptoms that may represent metastatic infection
medicationSafety: Vancomycin requires renal and exposure monitoring according to current protocol
Beta-lactam allergy history should be clarified rather than assumed
Linezolid has blood-count, serotonergic, and neuropathy considerations with longer use
teaching: Complete therapy and follow-up cultures/appointments; do not stop antibiotics when fever resolves
Use wound and hand-hygiene measures to reduce spread
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers ordered antimicrobials, monitors renal/infusion effects and source sites, maintains precautions, and escalates signs of metastatic infection. Antibiotic selection/duration and device removal are team decisions.
examTrap: Dismissing a blood culture growing S. aureus as contamination because only one bottle was initially positive.
oneLinePearl: S. aureus in blood deserves source, clearance, and complication follow-up.

title: HIV and ART: Viral Suppression Depends on Consistent Therapy
bottomLine: Modern antiretroviral therapy is continuous combination treatment aimed at durable viral suppression and immune preservation. Reinforce adherence, assess interactions and access barriers, monitor viral load/CD4 and medication-specific toxicity, and never recommend stopping ART because the patient feels well.
recognize: HIV may be asymptomatic for years without treatment
Viral load tracks treatment response; CD4 helps estimate immune status and opportunistic-infection risk
Treatment interruption can lead to viral rebound and resistance risk
assess: Medication list, adherence, side effects, access/cost, substance use and mental-health barriers without stigma
Trend viral load, CD4 and regimen-specific renal, hepatic, metabolic, or blood-count tests
Assess pregnancy potential and interacting medications/supplements
actions: Administer ART on schedule and resolve missed-dose/access barriers promptly
Use standard precautions; HIV does not require routine isolation
Support preventive care, STI testing, vaccination and opportunistic-infection prophylaxis when ordered
diagnostics: HIV antigen/antibody and nucleic-acid testing have different roles in diagnosis
An undetectable viral load on treatment reflects suppression, not eradication of HIV
medicationSafety: ART has major interaction potential with acid suppressants, anticonvulsants, rifamycins, polyvalent cations, and other drugs depending on regimen
Never assume all ART tablets can be crushed or administered through feeding tubes without pharmacy review
redFlags: Rapid weight loss or persistent fever
Treatment interruption due to access failure
teaching: Take ART consistently, keep viral-load follow-up, use current sexual-health prevention guidance, and discuss PrEP/PEP for partners or exposures with qualified clinicians
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN reinforces ART and prevention plans and identifies barriers/adverse effects. Regimen selection or resistance management is HIV-specialist/prescriber directed.
examTrap: Using special isolation precautions simply because a patient has HIV, rather than applying Standard Precautions based on exposure risk.
oneLinePearl: HIV treatment works when ART stays consistent and viral load stays suppressed.

title: Advanced HIV: Match the Symptom Pattern to the Opportunistic Risk
bottomLine: As immune suppression deepens, opportunistic infection and malignancy risk rises. In a patient with HIV, new dyspnea, focal neurologic change, severe headache, persistent diarrhea, visual symptoms, fever, weight loss or oral/esophageal symptoms require prompt evaluation rather than being labeled as a routine viral illness.
recognize: Pneumocystis pneumonia can cause progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fever and hypoxemia
Cryptococcal meningitis can cause headache and altered mental status
Toxoplasma can cause focal neurologic deficits or seizures
CMV can threaten vision in severe immune suppression
assess: Respiratory, neurologic, visual, GI and oral symptoms plus CD4/viral-load context
Medication adherence and prophylaxis history
Oxygenation and hemodynamic stability
actions: Escalate acute respiratory/neuro/visual deterioration
Administer organism-specific treatment and prophylaxis as ordered
Continue or coordinate ART according to the specialist treatment plan
Use transmission precautions based on the actual infection, not HIV status alone
diagnostics: Testing is syndrome-specific and may include imaging, CSF, respiratory specimens, antigen/PCR, ophthalmologic evaluation, or cultures
Do not delay emergency stabilization while waiting for an exact organism
medicationSafety: TMP-SMX, azoles, antivirals and other OI drugs have renal, hematologic, hepatic and interaction risks
Starting ART timing can require specialist coordination in selected CNS opportunistic infections because of immune reconstitution concerns
teaching: Keep ART and prophylaxis appointments; report new respiratory, neuro, visual or persistent systemic symptoms early
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN identifies syndrome patterns, monitors treatment and side effects, and escalates deterioration. OI diagnosis, prophylaxis thresholds and ART timing are specialist directed.
examTrap: Using HIV status alone to decide isolation precautions or assuming any pneumonia in HIV is automatically Pneumocystis.
oneLinePearl: Advanced HIV: new lungs, brain, eyes or persistent fever need an opportunistic-infection workup.
sourceBasis: U.S. Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Adults and Adolescents With HIV

title: Antibiotic Safety: Right Drug, Right Culture, Right Duration
bottomLine: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, not every fever or positive culture. Obtain indicated cultures before therapy when feasible, give time-critical empiric antibiotics promptly for severe infection, then reassess culture data, source control, renal function, toxicity and whether therapy can be narrowed or stopped.
recognize: Broad-spectrum therapy may be necessary initially in severe infection but should not stay broad by inertia
Colonization or contamination can produce positive cultures without clinical infection
Antibiotic exposure can cause C. difficile, drug reactions and resistant organisms
assess: Allergy history and reaction type, renal/hepatic function, infection site, culture results, clinical response
IV site/line and infusion reactions
Diarrhea, rash, kidney injury, blood-count or neurologic toxicity depending on agent
actions: Give antimicrobials at the prescribed dose/time
Collect cultures correctly when ordered
Report culture/susceptibility results and lack of clinical response
Support IV-to-oral transition and de-escalation when the care plan changes
diagnostics: Culture and susceptibility results guide narrowing
Procalcitonin or other biomarkers supplement clinical judgment; they do not replace source assessment
medicationSafety: Dose adjustment is common in renal dysfunction
Multiple antibiotics can prolong QT, suppress marrow, injure kidney/liver, or interact with other drugs
Do not document every GI upset as a true antibiotic allergy without clarification
redFlags: New focal infection needing source control
teaching: Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed, do not share leftovers, and report serious allergy or severe diarrhea
Explain that narrower therapy after cultures is good stewardship, not weaker care
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers antibiotics, monitors response/toxicity, and communicates cultures and adverse effects. Selection/de-escalation requires prescriber/pharmacy authorization.
examTrap: Assuming the broadest antibiotic regimen is always the safest even after cultures identify a narrower effective option.
oneLinePearl: Start fast when severe, then narrow smart when data arrive.

title: Central-Line Infection: Protect the Line and Recognize Bloodstream Sepsis
bottomLine: Central lines create direct bloodstream access. Use strict aseptic hub and dressing technique, reassess whether the line is still needed, and treat fever, chills with infusion, site drainage, unexplained sepsis, or new line dysfunction as possible catheter-related infection until evaluated.
recognize: Exit-site redness, drainage, tenderness, or tunnel symptoms
Fever/rigors during line use can signal bloodstream infection
Bloodstream infection can occur without obvious local redness
assess: Line site/dressing, necessity, tubing/connections, patient temperature and hemodynamics
Review blood cultures, line cultures when ordered, and other infection sources
Assess for thrombosis or mechanical complications
actions: Perform hand hygiene and disinfect access hubs using the approved method
Maintain sterile dressing and closed system
Collect ordered cultures correctly and give antibiotics promptly when infection suspected
Prepare for line removal/exchange if ordered
diagnostics: Blood cultures from peripheral and/or line sites may help identify catheter-related bloodstream infection according to protocol
Do not routinely culture asymptomatic lines
medicationSafety: Antibiotic lock therapy is indication- and device-specific and should not be improvised
Line incompatibilities and lumen assignment require pharmacy/policy review
teaching: Keep dressing dry/intact, use hand hygiene, and report fever, chills during infusion, drainage, or line damage
scopeAndDelegation: Central-line access and dressing roles vary by state and competency. PN/LVN should never perform a restricted central-line procedure merely because peripheral IV skills are authorized.
examTrap: Accessing a central line with rushed hub cleaning because the patient urgently needs medication.
oneLinePearl: Central line: scrub, sterile, necessity—and take fever seriously.
sourceBasis: CDC Guidelines for Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections

title: Systemic Lupus: Flare, Infection, Kidney, Clot, and Pregnancy Risk
bottomLine: SLE is multisystem autoimmune disease. New fatigue, rash, arthritis or serologic activity may be a flare, but fever and organ dysfunction in an immunosuppressed patient can also be infection. Watch kidneys, CNS, blood counts, thrombosis risk and pregnancy complications; do not automatically increase immunosuppression before infection is considered.
recognize: Photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, inflammatory arthritis, serositis, cytopenias
Lupus nephritis can cause proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension and kidney dysfunction
Antiphospholipid antibodies can increase thrombosis/pregnancy risk
assess: Vitals, infection symptoms, skin/joints, neuro status, edema/BP/urine
CBC, creatinine, urinalysis/protein, complement/autoantibody trends as ordered
Medication adherence and steroid/immunosuppressive toxicity
actions: Administer hydroxychloroquine/immunosuppression as ordered and monitor toxicity
Use sun protection and cardiovascular/infection prevention
Escalate nephritis, neuro symptoms, thrombosis, severe cytopenia or infection
diagnostics: Autoantibodies support diagnosis but symptoms and organ testing determine current clinical problems
Urine protein and renal evaluation matter in suspected nephritis
medicationSafety: Hydroxychloroquine requires retinal-toxicity monitoring
Steroids and immunosuppressants raise infection and metabolic risks
Pregnancy safety differs significantly among immunosuppressants
redFlags: Pregnancy with severe hypertension or organ flare
teaching: Sun protection, medication adherence, vaccine/infection planning, pregnancy planning with rheumatology/obstetrics, and early reporting of organ symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors symptoms, renal/BP trends, infection and medication toxicity and reinforces the established plan. Immunosuppressive regimen changes are specialist directed.
examTrap: Assuming every fever in a patient with lupus is a flare and giving more immunosuppression without assessing infection.
oneLinePearl: Lupus can flare, infect, clot, or injure kidneys—figure out which problem is active.
sourceBasis: American College of Rheumatology SLE/lupus nephritis guidance

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Control Inflammation, Preserve Function, Watch Immunosuppression
bottomLine: Rheumatoid arthritis is systemic inflammatory disease, not simply age-related joint wear. Disease-modifying therapy protects joints and function; nursing priorities include pain/fatigue management, safe activity, infection monitoring, medication toxicity, and recognizing cervical spine or systemic complications.
recognize: Symmetric inflammatory small-joint pain/swelling and prolonged morning stiffness
Fatigue and systemic inflammation
Chronic disease can cause deformity, nodules, lung/eye/cardiovascular involvement
assess: Pain/swelling, morning stiffness, mobility/function and fatigue
Infection signs before/during immunosuppressive therapy
CBC, liver, renal and other medication-specific monitoring
actions: Balance activity and rest; use PT/OT and joint-protection strategies
Administer DMARD/biologic therapy as ordered
Escalate severe infection and new neurologic symptoms in longstanding cervical disease
diagnostics: RF and anti-CCP support diagnosis but are not perfect standalone tests
Inflammatory markers help follow disease in context
medicationSafety: Methotrexate has liver, marrow, pulmonary and pregnancy risks and is generally weekly, not daily, for RA
Biologics/JAK inhibitors increase infection risks and require screening/monitoring
NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not stop joint damage
teaching: Keep DMARD monitoring, vaccines as advised before/during immunosuppression, smoking cessation, exercise/joint protection, and pregnancy planning
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors functional status and medication toxicity and reinforces treatment. DMARD selection and dosing are rheumatology/prescriber decisions.
examTrap: Teaching a patient to take methotrexate daily when the RA prescription is weekly.
oneLinePearl: RA needs disease-modifying therapy; pain control alone does not protect joints.
sourceBasis: American College of Rheumatology Rheumatoid Arthritis Guideline

title: Immunosuppression and Vaccines: Live vs Non-Live Matters
bottomLine: Immunosuppressive medications and conditions change vaccine timing and which vaccines are safe. Inactivated/non-live vaccines are generally usable but immune response may be reduced; live vaccines may be contraindicated during significant immunosuppression. Verify the exact therapy, immune status and current CDC schedule rather than using one blanket rule.
recognize: High-dose systemic steroids, biologics, transplant drugs, chemotherapy and severe immune deficiencies can alter vaccine recommendations
Some vaccines are best given before immunosuppression when time allows
Household-contact recommendations can also differ for selected live vaccines
assess: Medication name/dose/timing, immune condition, pregnancy, prior vaccines and infection history
Check current CDC immunization recommendations and specialty plan
Assess fever/acute illness when deciding same-day administration
actions: Administer indicated vaccines at safe timing according to current schedule and specialist plan
Defer contraindicated live vaccines and clarify with the care team
Use post-exposure prophylaxis/immunoglobulin when indicated
diagnostics: Serologic testing for immunity is recommended only in selected situations; do not order blanket titers for every vaccine
medicationSafety: Biologic immune therapies and timing around B-cell-depleting agents can reduce vaccine response
Do not confuse a non-live recombinant vaccine with a live vaccine based on the disease name alone
redFlags: Unrecognized live-vaccine administration during profound immunosuppression
teaching: Keep a vaccine record and discuss vaccines before starting immunosuppression, travel, pregnancy, or transplant therapy
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN may administer vaccines under standing orders where authorized, but contraindication screening and current schedule verification are essential. Complex immunosuppression timing should be clarified before administration.
examTrap: Assuming every vaccine is contraindicated because a patient is immunosuppressed.
oneLinePearl: Immunosuppression changes timing and live-vaccine safety—not the value of vaccination.
sourceBasis: CDC Adult Immunization Schedule and Altered Immunocompetence Guidance

title: Solid-Organ Transplant: Rejection, Infection, and Drug Toxicity Overlap
bottomLine: After transplant, fever, graft dysfunction, pain, fluid changes or abnormal labs can reflect rejection, infection, medication toxicity, obstruction or vascular complications. Never tell a transplant recipient to stop immunosuppression because of infection symptoms; urgent transplant-team assessment is needed to balance both risks.
recognize: Rejection presentation depends on the transplanted organ and may be subtle
Immunosuppression can blunt fever and inflammatory signs
Calcineurin inhibitors can injure kidneys and cause neurologic/metabolic effects
assess: Vitals, infection symptoms, graft-specific function, medication adherence/timing
Trend drug levels and renal, liver, electrolyte, glucose, CBC tests as ordered
Review interacting drugs, grapefruit/products when relevant to the specific agent, and missed doses
actions: Contact transplant team promptly for fever or graft dysfunction
Administer immunosuppressants exactly on schedule
Use infection prevention and prophylaxis as ordered
Escalate sepsis or acute graft failure
diagnostics: Drug levels, imaging, cultures and biopsy are used according to the graft problem
Abnormal creatinine after kidney transplant is not automatically rejection
medicationSafety: Tacrolimus/cyclosporine have major interaction, kidney, neuro and electrolyte risks
Mycophenolate has marrow, GI and pregnancy toxicity
Never substitute formulations or change timing casually because drug exposure matters
teaching: Never miss or stop anti-rejection medication without transplant-team instructions, keep lab/drug-level follow-up, use infection precautions and sun protection as advised
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN emphasizes exact medication timing, lab/toxicity monitoring and prompt transplant-team communication. Immunosuppression adjustment is specialist directed.
examTrap: Holding tacrolimus for fever without an order because immunosuppression seems unsafe during infection.
oneLinePearl: Transplant fever or dysfunction needs the transplant team—do not independently stop anti-rejection drugs.
sourceBasis: U.S. transplant infectious disease and immunosuppression practice guidance

title: Medication and Latex Allergy: Clarify the Reaction Before You Label the Risk
bottomLine: An allergy label should record the substance and the actual reaction. Distinguish expected side effects or intolerance from immediate hypersensitivity, while taking prior anaphylaxis or severe cutaneous reactions seriously. For true latex allergy, create a latex-safe environment and avoid unnecessary exposure.
recognize: Immediate allergy can cause hives, angioedema, wheeze or anaphylaxis
Severe delayed reactions such as SJS/TEN or DRESS are different from nausea or diarrhea
Latex sensitivity can occur with repeated healthcare exposure and selected cross-reactive fruit allergies but fruit sensitivity alone does not diagnose latex allergy
assess: Exact drug/product, timing, symptoms, treatment required, and whether the patient has tolerated related agents since
Check chart/wristband and procedure supplies
Assess airway and hemodynamics immediately for active severe reaction
actions: Stop the suspected triggering exposure
Treat anaphylaxis with epinephrine/emergency pathway
Use latex-safe supplies when a true latex allergy is documented
Update allergy documentation with reaction details
diagnostics: Allergy testing or specialist challenge is selected by the allergy team; do not deliberately re-expose a patient to a severe reaction at bedside
medicationSafety: Do not relabel predictable side effects as anaphylaxis without clarification
Severe cutaneous adverse-reaction histories can make re-exposure dangerous even without immediate IgE symptoms
redFlags: Medication re-exposure after a severe documented reaction
teaching: Know the exact allergy and reaction, carry epinephrine when prescribed, and communicate serious allergy before procedures or new medications
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN obtains accurate allergy history, avoids documented triggers, administers emergency therapy under protocol, and reports serious reactions. Drug-allergy delabeling/testing is specialist directed.
examTrap: Documenting 'allergy' with no reaction details after a patient reports nausea from an antibiotic, or ignoring a prior severe skin reaction because it was not immediate.
oneLinePearl: Allergy safety starts with the reaction story, not just the label.
sourceBasis: AAAAI/ACAAI Drug Allergy and Anaphylaxis Practice Parameters
